title: Marguerite and the Well
premise: Folklorist Jude Vasquez returns to the village of Hollowmere to record a harvest song that locals will sing once but never repeat, and finds their childhood imaginary friend, Marguerite, waiting on the porch — unchanged after twenty years. As Jude transcribes the song, they discover it is a counting rhyme that names villagers before they vanish, and that their own name appears in a verse dated for this autumn. The well at the village center is not a well but a mouth, and everything the village has forgotten has been swallowed into it, including, Jude learns, the sibling they were made to forget. To save themselves and the village's stolen memories, Jude must learn the song's final verse from Marguerite without ever singing along, then carry it down into the well and give it back to the thing below — trading their own remembered childhood as payment.
about_author: Kestrel Nystrom is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in remote coastal settlements before turning to fiction. They write horror about the things communities agree not to remember, and live within earshot of the sea.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Jude Vasquez arrives in Hollowmere after a decade away, ostensibly to record folk songs for an archive. At the tavern, an old woman sings the harvest song beautifully once; when Jude asks her to repeat it, the room goes silent and she leaves without a word. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: unease dressed up as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Marguerite on the Porch
chapters.summary: At the rented cottage, Jude finds Marguerite — the imaginary friend from childhood, a girl in a yellow raincoat — sitting on the porch steps, exactly as remembered, unaged. She says only, 'You came back late.' Jude convinces themselves it's stress, a hallucination, anything. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: uncanny dread colliding with a strange, guilty relief.

chapters.title: What the Archive Doesn't Hold
chapters.summary: Jude reviews their own decade-old field recordings from Hollowmere and finds gaps: interviews that skip mid-sentence, a child's voice on one tape asking 'where's the other one?' Jude cannot recall recording any children. POV: Jude, with tape transcripts interleaved. Emotional beat: the ground shifting under their own memory.

chapters.title: The Counting Verse
chapters.summary: Jude persuades the innkeeper, Bram, to hum the harvest song's melody. He does, then goes pale: the lyrics are a counting rhyme, and each number carries a villager's name. The last name sung was his brother's, thirty years ago. POV: Bram, briefly, then Jude. Emotional beat: horror becoming communal, no longer private.

chapters.title: Yellow Raincoat
chapters.summary: Marguerite begins appearing indoors, always slightly closer than expected, always patient. She tells Jude the song has a last verse nobody sings, and that Jude knew it once. When pressed, she recites the first line — in Jude's own voice. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: terror braided with longing for something lost.

chapters.title: The Well at the Center
chapters.summary: Jude visits the old stone well on the green, capped with an iron grate since before anyone remembers. A child nearby says matter-of-factly that you mustn't lean over it because 'it leans back.' That night, Jude dreams of standing at its lip, being looked at. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: the village's fear revealed as inherited, rational survival knowledge.

chapters.title: Names in Order
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing parish records with the rhyme's verses, Jude maps each named person to a date of disappearance or departure — every one real, every one erased from local memory afterward. The next verse contains a name Jude recognizes with a sick lurch: their own childhood nickname. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: cold, methodical dread.

chapters.title: The Empty Bedroom
chapters.summary: Marguerite leads Jude, wordlessly, to the cottage's sealed back bedroom, where they find two beds, two sets of childhood drawings, and evidence of a second child who lived here. Jude's mother's letters mention only one. Marguerite says, 'You promised you'd remember.' POV: Jude. Emotional beat: grief for a loss they cannot yet name.

chapters.title: Bram's Confession
chapters.summary: Drunk and terrified, Bram tells Jude what the village elders know: the well takes a name when the song names it, and the village survives by forgetting. His brother didn't leave; he was given. Some families, he hints, gave more than others. He looks at Jude when he says it. POV: Bram. Emotional beat: complicity surfacing like a drowned body.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't Sung
chapters.summary: In the archive of a defunct chapel, Jude finds a hymnal with the harvest song written out — ending mid-line at the final verse, the rest scraped away by many hands over generations. Beneath the scraping, faint pencil: a single instruction. 'Learn it whole. Never sing it.' POV: Jude. Emotional beat: hope arriving wearing warning colors.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Terms
chapters.summary: Marguerite finally explains: she is what the well returned instead of taking — a memory given shape so someone wouldn't be wholly forgotten. She can teach Jude the last verse, but only if Jude never sings along, never completes it aloud, or the giving starts early. POV: Jude, with Marguerite's alien calm pressing against the narration. Emotional beat: trust extended across an impossible gulf.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Nightly lessons begin. Marguerite sings; Jude listens, mouths nothing, writes everything down. Each session, fragments of Jude's suppressed childhood surface — a swing, a fever, a small hand in theirs. The village watches Jude with new attention. Someone has scratched out the nickname in the parish register. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: intimacy and countdown intertwined.

chapters.title: The One Who Leans
chapters.summary: The well's grate is found open, folded back neatly like a page. Villagers begin humming the song involuntarily in their sleep; three report dreaming of a figure standing in their yards, listening. Jude realizes the thing below knows someone is learning the verse. POV: rotating village voices, then Jude. Emotional beat: siege atmosphere, the community fracturing.

chapters.title: What Mother Gave
chapters.summary: Among the mother's letters, Jude deciphers the truth: there were two children. When the song named the younger one, the mother bargained — offering the elder child's memories of the younger in exchange for delay. Jude's entire childhood was edited. Marguerite is stitched from what remained. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: devastation reframing every prior chapter.

chapters.title: The Name in the Next Verse
chapters.summary: Autumn deepens. The rhyme, sung once at the harvest fire as tradition demands, gains a new line overnight: Jude's full name now sits where the nickname used to be. The village, gently, terribly, begins treating Jude as already gone — setting no place for them at table. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: social death preceding the literal one.

chapters.title: Run
chapters.summary: Jude tries to leave. Every road out of Hollowmere curves back to the green; the bus arrives empty and departs without them. Marguerite waits at the crossroads, rain-soaked, saying the verse can't be learned anywhere but here, because the song is the village and the village is the song. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: claustrophobic despair hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Marguerite teaches the final verse completely — the verse that returns what was taken, at the price of the singer's dearest memory. Jude memorizes it in silence, hour after hour, while Marguerite grows fainter with each repetition, spending herself. She asks Jude to remember her too, if there's room left. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: tender, unbearable farewell-in-advance.

chapters.title: Harvest Night
chapters.summary: On the night the song is due, the village gathers at the well, compelled, faces slack, singing the naming verses in unison as the grate groans open. The thing below rises through the sound itself. Jude walks to the lip carrying the unsung verse like a lit coal. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into ceremony.

chapters.title: Down the Throat of It
chapters.summary: Climax. Jude descends into the well and, inside the dark, meets the accumulated forgotten — including, briefly, the sibling, still seven years old, waiting. Jude speaks the last verse aloud, whole, alone, giving the thing below its own name back and demanding the trade: everything taken, for everything Jude remembers of childhood. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: sacrifice as an act of fierce love.

chapters.title: The Return
chapters.summary: Dawn. Jude climbs out of a dry, ordinary stone well. Around the green, villagers wake weeping, remembering brothers, daughters, neighbors — decades of stolen names flooding home. The harvest song now ends where it should. Jude remembers almost nothing of their own first ten years, and cannot picture Marguerite's face at all. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: hollow, luminous aftermath.

chapters.title: Two Beds
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Jude stays on, restoring the cottage. The back bedroom is opened, aired, furnished with two beds again. The sibling — grown now, living down the coast — writes a cautious letter: 'I don't know why I'm writing, but I keep dreaming about a swing.' Jude begins to answer. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: grief learning to become relationship.

chapters.title: The Song You Sing Twice
chapters.summary: At the next harvest, the village sings the whole song together, twice, loudly, as defiance and thanks. On the porch afterward, Jude finds a yellow raincoat hanging on the rail, dry despite the drizzle, and — for one breath — hears a small voice finish the last line with them. Some things given away find their way back smaller, and stay. POV: Jude. Emotional beat: earned, fragile belonging; memory chosen rather than owed.
